paragraphs.title: The Source of the Proverbs, Mystery, and Rulership

answers: The men of Hezekiah king of Judah
The men of David king of Israel
easy.explanation: Verse 1 says they were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah.
easy.q: Who copied out these proverbs of Solomon?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “It is the glory of God to conceal a thing.”
easy.q: What is the glory of God?

easy.explanation: Verse 5 says, “Take away the wicked from before the king.”
easy.q: What must be taken away for the king’s throne to be established in righteousness?

answers: God conceals, while kings search out matters
medium.explanation: The verse contrasts God’s glory in concealing with the honour of kings in searching out a matter.
medium.q: What contrast does verse 2 make between God and kings?

medium.explanation: Dross is the unwanted impurity removed from silver.
medium.q: What does “dross” mean in the phrase “Take away the dross from the silver”?

medium.explanation: As dross is removed from silver, wickedness is removed so the throne may be established in righteousness.
medium.q: What relationship do the verses show between removing wickedness and government?

answers: Searching the depths of the earth
challenge.explanation: The refining of silver pictures removing wickedness from before the king.
challenge.q: What image describes preparing a kingdom for righteous rule?

answers: Only the earth cannot be searched
Some things are too deep to be fully searched out
challenge.explanation: The heart of kings is described as unsearchable, like the height of heaven and depth of earth.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the heaven, earth, and heart of kings?

answers: It is part of their duty to discern and establish just rule
It replaces the need for righteousness
challenge.explanation: The verse presents investigation as an honour of kings, followed by the removal of wickedness.
challenge.q: Why is searching out a matter called the honour of kings?

paragraphs.title: Humility, Status, and Caution in Conflict

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Put not forth thyself in the presence of the king.”
easy.q: What should a person not do in the presence of a king?

easy.explanation: The passage warns against going forth hastily to strive.
easy.q: What should be done instead of going hastily to strive?

easy.explanation: Verse 9 says, “discover not a secret to another.”
easy.q: What must not be discovered to another during a dispute?

answers: He may be put lower and humbled
medium.explanation: It is better to be invited upward than to be put lower before the prince.
medium.q: What may happen to someone who puts himself forward before a ruler without invitation?

medium.explanation: Here, to strive means to enter into a quarrel or dispute.
medium.q: What does “strive” mean in this passage?

answers: The dispute may bring greater honour
A neighbour may shame him in the end
A quarrel always brings an invitation
medium.explanation: The verse warns that a neighbour may put him to shame.
medium.q: Why should a person avoid going hastily to strive?

challenge.explanation: Both instructions require humility and control rather than impulsive action.
challenge.q: What quality is common to the warnings against self-display and rash quarrelling?

answers: A quarrel permits every secret to be revealed
Even during a dispute, secrets should be protected
Secrets have no connection with disputes
challenge.explanation: The passage permits debating one’s cause but forbids discovering a secret to another.
challenge.q: What connection does the passage make between quarrelling and secrets?

answers: Put forward, quarrel, and reveal secrets
Wait humbly, avoid rash conflict, and guard secrets
Question the king and demand an invitation
challenge.explanation: These are the connected instructions in verses 6–10.
challenge.q: What order of conduct is suggested for someone dealing with important people?

paragraphs.title: Right Words, Rebuke, and Faithful Service

answers: Apples of gold in pictures of silver
easy.explanation: Verse 11 says, “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.”
easy.q: What are fitly spoken words compared to?

easy.explanation: A faithful messenger refreshes the soul of his masters.
easy.q: What does a faithful messenger do for those who send him?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “a soft tongue breaketh the bone.”
easy.q: What can break the bone?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes speech given in the right way and at the right time.
medium.q: What does “a word fitly spoken” mean?

answers: Only a willing hearer can receive correction
Reproof is not for wise people
medium.explanation: The image is of wise correction being received by a responsive listener.
medium.q: Why does a wise reprover need an obedient ear?

medium.explanation: The messenger refreshes the soul, while the soft tongue has persuasive power.
medium.q: What do a faithful messenger and a soft tongue have in common?

answers: Both are valuable when presented in the proper setting
challenge.explanation: Beautiful speech and fitting correction are valuable when appropriately given.
challenge.q: What similarity exists between the golden apples and wise reproof?

answers: Faithfulness refreshes, while false promises disappoint
Both benefit those who send them
Only the messenger must avoid speaking
challenge.explanation: A faithful messenger refreshes, but a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain.
challenge.q: What contrast is shown between a faithful messenger and one who boasts of a false gift?

answers: They can influence even a difficult ruler
They remove the need for correction
They cause people to promise gifts
challenge.explanation: Long forbearing persuades a prince, and a soft tongue breaks the bone.
challenge.q: How do patience and gentle speech work together?

paragraphs.title: Proper Measure in Relationships and Actions

answers: Eat as much as is sufficient
easy.explanation: The verse says, “eat so much as is sufficient for thee.”
easy.q: What should a person do after finding honey?

answers: The neighbour may become weary and hate him
The neighbour will give faithful testimony
The neighbour will invite him before the king
easy.explanation: The passage warns that the neighbour may become weary and hate him.
easy.q: What may happen if someone visits a neighbour’s house too often?

easy.explanation: False witness is compared to a maul, a sword, and a sharp arrow.
easy.q: What does the verse condemn?

medium.explanation: The instruction means not to overstay or visit excessively.
medium.q: What does “Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour’s house” mean?

answers: It may cause a person to vomit
medium.explanation: The verse warns that being filled with honey may result in vomiting.
medium.q: Why is eating too much honey harmful?

answers: Things that cannot be relied upon
medium.explanation: Each image describes something unstable or unreliable in time of trouble.
medium.q: What do a broken tooth, a foot out of joint, and an unfaithful man represent?

challenge.explanation: The verses warn against excess in honey and visits and against trusting an unfaithful person.
challenge.q: What principle is shared by honey, visiting, and relying on a person?

answers: It may ignore the person’s condition instead of fitting it
It causes honey to be vomited
challenge.explanation: The comparison teaches that a response should suit the person’s condition.
challenge.q: Why may singing songs be unsuitable for a heavy heart?

answers: Both can cause harm in a time of need
challenge.explanation: False witness harms a neighbour, while an unfaithful man cannot be trusted in trouble.
challenge.q: What connects false testimony with confidence in an unfaithful man?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat.”
easy.q: What should be given to an enemy who is hungry?

easy.explanation: The verse commands, “if he be thirsty, give him water to drink.”
easy.q: What should be given to an enemy who is thirsty?

easy.explanation: Verse 22 says, “the LORD shall reward thee.”
easy.q: Who will reward the person who shows this kindness?

answers: When he asks for a secret
medium.explanation: The command begins, “If thine enemy be hungry.”
medium.q: Under what condition should an enemy be given bread?

answers: Kindness may bring shame or conviction
medium.explanation: The image presents kindness as having a humbling or convicting effect.
medium.q: What does heaping coals of fire upon an enemy’s head represent here?

answers: The enemy is humbled, and the giver is rewarded by the LORD
The enemy is strengthened, and the giver is punished
medium.explanation: The passage mentions coals upon his head and the LORD’s reward.
medium.q: What two results are associated with helping an enemy?

answers: Kindness is not limited only to those who love us
Kindness is permitted only toward kings
challenge.explanation: The command expressly extends practical help even to an enemy.
challenge.q: What does this command teach about the limits of kindness?

answers: They answer the needs of hunger and thirst
They compare kings and poor people
They teach how to prepare a feast
challenge.explanation: Bread is given to the hungry and water to the thirsty.
challenge.q: Why are both bread and water mentioned?

challenge.explanation: The passage concludes, “the LORD shall reward thee.”
challenge.q: What higher motive is given at the end of the passage?

easy.explanation: Verse 23 says, “The north wind driveth away rain.”
easy.q: What does the north wind drive away?

easy.explanation: The verse compares an angry countenance with a backbiting tongue.
easy.q: What is connected with an angry countenance?

answers: Dwelling in the corner of the housetop
Living in a house full of strife
easy.explanation: Verse 24 says it is better to dwell in the corner of the housetop.
easy.q: What is better than living in a wide house with a brawling woman?

medium.explanation: Brawling describes contentious or quarrelsome behavior.
medium.q: What does “brawling” mean in the phrase “a brawling woman”?

answers: Visible anger is linked with secret harmful speech
An angry face prevents all speech
medium.explanation: The verse places the angry countenance and backbiting tongue together.
medium.q: What connection does the verse make between an angry countenance and a backbiting tongue?

answers: It is quieter than a house filled with quarrelling
It is richer than a wide house
It is better for eating honey
medium.explanation: The comparison prefers quiet solitude to a home filled with contention.
medium.q: Why is the housetop corner preferable?

answers: Anger and strife create harm, so peaceful distance may be better
More quarrelling is needed to solve problems
Secret speech is always better than open speech
challenge.explanation: Both verses portray harmful conflict and favor separation from it.
challenge.q: What common idea appears in both verses?

answers: Quiet solitude versus a house full of quarrels
challenge.explanation: The verse contrasts a lonely but peaceful place with a spacious contentious home.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast in the verse about the housetop?

answers: Hidden speech can have a spreading effect like weather
All hidden speech is good news
challenge.explanation: The comparison links a natural force with the damaging effect of backbiting.
challenge.q: What may be inferred from the comparison involving the north wind and a backbiting tongue?

paragraphs.title: Good News, the Fall of the Righteous, and Self-Control

answers: Cold waters to a thirsty soul
easy.explanation: Verse 25 compares good news to cold waters for a thirsty soul.
easy.q: What is good news from a far country compared to?

easy.explanation: Verse 26 speaks of “A righteous man falling down before the wicked.”
easy.q: What may happen to a righteous man before the wicked?

answers: A city broken down and without walls
easy.explanation: The final verse compares such a person to an unwalled, broken-down city.
easy.q: What is a person without rule over his own spirit like?

medium.explanation: A troubled fountain is one that has become disturbed or corrupted.
medium.q: What does “a troubled fountain” describe?

answers: Both require moderation and should not be excessive
medium.explanation: The verse warns against excess in honey and excessive self-glory.
medium.q: What connection is made between eating much honey and searching one’s own glory?

answers: He knows how to investigate matters
medium.explanation: A broken-down city without walls pictures a person who lacks inner defense and control.
medium.q: What does the image of a city without walls teach about a person without self-control?

answers: Both refresh and revive a weary or thirsty soul
challenge.explanation: Good news is compared with refreshing cold water.
challenge.q: What connection exists between good news and cold waters?

answers: The corruption of something that should be clean and stable
The increase of the righteous man’s honour
challenge.explanation: Both images portray damage to something that ought to be pure or secure.
challenge.q: What does the troubled fountain beside the falling righteous man represent?

answers: Both warn against a lack of moderation
Both command people to reveal secrets
challenge.explanation: Excessive honey and an unrestrained spirit both illustrate the danger of lacking self-control.
challenge.q: How do the ending verses connect with the warning about excessive honey?
